newsitem.title: CANADA: Upstart Canada gas pipeline dies on drawing board.
newsitem.headline: Upstart Canada gas pipeline dies on drawing board.

text.p: A second natural gas pipeline proposal that would have competed with NOVA Corp on its exclusive Alberta home turf died on the drawing board on Friday in a victory for NOVA.
But analysts said NOVA Gas Transmission, which operates Alberta's sole gas pipeline network, still faces its biggest competitive challenge -- the proposed C$3.6-billion Alliance Pipeline.
The Alberta Pipeline Project, planned by ATCO Ltd unit ATCO Gas Pipelines and Shell Canada Ltd, said on Friday it canceled its plans to build a 1.2 billion cubic feet per day line in central Alberta.

The ill-fated project was first announced late last year, just days after another pipeline that would have chewed into NOVA's revenues -- the Palliser Pipeline -- was scrapped when its backers struck a cheaper transport toll deal with NOVA.

APP, which at the outset believed it had enough gas committed to the C$450 million project from its heavyweight partners, said things changed over the past six months and an unsuccessful open season left it short of firm commitments from producers.
"They weren't there in the end," project leader Larry Graburn said in a phone interview.

The project was first proposed by ATCO, Shell and Amoco Corp unit Amoco Canada Petroleum Co Ltd. Amoco later pulled its ownership stake from the project but said it still planned to be a big shipper on the line.
Another major oil company, Mobil Corp unit Mobil Oil Canada, said it would pledge gas volumes to APP.
A week after it pulled out of APP, Amoco announced it struck a deal to build a chemical plant in central Alberta adjecent to a NOVA petrochemical complex.
Amoco's cut in support for APP did not in itself kill APP, but "for sure, it was a factor," Graburn said.

He also said changes to tolling structure now expected from NOVA when its one-size-fits-all "postage stamp" rates become a thing of the past may have swayed prospective shippers from the upstart project.

"If you look at NOVA's plans going forward they seem to be much more aggressive economically than they have been in the past, so I think Alliance and other pipelines like ourselves may have had an impact on how they go forward," Graburn said.

Producer-backed Alliance, which would move 1.3 billion cubic feet of gas a day to Chicago from northern Canada in competition with major pipeline firms like NOVA and TransCanada PipeLines Ltd, filed its application Thursday with Canada's National Energy Board.
In its filing, Alliance said it had an impressive 98 percent of its capacity committed to 15-year contracts.

"How you derail Alliance is the thing NOVA really has to think about," said ScotiaMcleod analyst Sam Kanes, who gives Alliance a 60 to 70 percent chance of being built on the strength of its signed shipper commitments.
"So far, in some form, Alliance has a pretty decent shot at proceeding," Kanes said.

NOVA spokesman Paul Clark said his firm continues to discuss with its customers plans for new tolling and other services in the dying days of postage stamp tolls, in which producers pay the same to ship on the system regardless of where the gas is produced. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
